core_insight: API versioning decouples producer and consumer release cycles by keeping multiple contract versions alive in parallel, routing callers to the version they understand, and retiring old versions on a schedule.

scenes.voice: Here’s the uncomfortable truth about APIs: once you ship a shape, thousands of clients start depending on it.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a POST /orders request with fields {item, qty} being called by multiple client icons. A red warning appears as a field is crossed out.

scenes.voice: Product wants to add price, rename qty to quantity, change error codes. You can’t update every mobile app and partner at once.
scenes.visual: Timeline showing mobile app updates lagging months, internal services deploying on different cadences, partner SLA badge.

scenes.voice: The real problem isn’t change. It’s the constraint: ship new behavior while old clients keep working, without forking your codebase into unmaintainable copies.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left shows new feature request, right shows old client breaking with error icon. A scale balances 'evolve' vs 'breakage'.

scenes.voice: The obvious fix is strict backward compatibility: only add optional fields, never rename. That works for small internal teams, but fails when semantics must change.
scenes.visual: Code diff showing only additive optional fields. Then a red X over a rename from qty to quantity.
scenes.on_screen_text: Backward compat only → hits a wall

scenes.voice: Versioning is time travel for your contract. Keep v1 and v2 alive in parallel. The client promises which contract it speaks, the gateway routes to the right implementation.
scenes.visual: Simple flowchart animating client promises to router to service versions.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    ClientA -->|v1| Router
    ClientB -->|v2| Router
    Router -->|route| Service_v1
    Router -->|route| Service_v2
    Service_v1 --> DB
    Service_v2 --> DB

scenes.voice: Version can be in the URI like /v1/orders, a header like Accept-Version, or content negotiation. Pick one visible scheme early and stick with it.
scenes.visual: Three request examples highlighting URI, header, and Accept media type.

scenes.voice: You gain independent release cycles. You pay for it with version explosion, data model drift, and ops overhead. The hidden cost is adapters that map a single domain model to multiple contract shapes.
scenes.visual: Domain model in center with adapters branching to v1 and v2 response shapes. Metrics dashboard shows requests per version.

scenes.voice: Version when you have external consumers, long-lived clients, or independent teams. Monitor usage per version and retire aggressively. Keeping old versions is a liability.
scenes.visual: Deprecation timeline with traffic dropping below 1% and a sunset icon.

mental_model: Think of versioning as decoupling release cycles via explicit client promises. Client declares version → Gateway routes → Implementation evolves. Compatibility cost lives in adapters and data model, not just routing. Retire versions on metrics, not feelings.
final_takeaway: Versioning exists to decouple producer and consumer release cycles. Ship new behavior without breaking old clients, and retire old versions on a schedule.
